## Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

### How the phase ends (changed)

By the end of July 1965 the advisory war is over. The decision to commit US ground forces in strength has been taken, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and the III Marine Amphibious Force are in the country, the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) is preparing to sail, and Rolling Thunder is in its fifth month. On the other side, the Viet Cong have formed regiments and divisions in the provinces around Saigon and in the coastal lowlands, PAVN regular regiments are in the Central Highlands, and the summer offensive has broken ARVN battalions at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai faster than they could be rebuilt, though none of the general reserve has been wiped out. In the countryside, the Viet Cong infrastructure administers, taxes and conscripts in a large share of the hamlets, and outside the held belt the government's pacification effort has nothing like the stable administration or the local security it needs. Inside it the summer is not the historical one: about 330,000 hectares of rice land have been titled to about 270,000 families, rent is no longer paid in most of the districts the government holds, and in those districts the government's arrival no longer means the landlord's¹. Where the government does not hold the hamlets at night, nothing has changed except the promise.

In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta has just taken power after a year and a half of coups. In Washington, the war has an open-ended authority from Congress and a decision on troops announced without the reserves, without a tax increase and without a declaration. In Hanoi, the Politburo has committed itself to winning before the Americans arrive in strength and must now decide whether to fight them. It will: in October the PAVN regiments of the B3 Front will go after the camp at Plei Me, and the Ia Drang will follow. The war that Phase II inherits is a war between two armies that each believe they can outlast the other, fought over a population that neither government has secured.

About 1,100 village posts are settled, two-thirds of the chiefs have come from the list, and the infrastructure has begun to leave the villages around the posts². The sea route to the coast is closed and the Cambodian route open, and the enemy's rear is on the U-2S's maps while his regiments under the canopy and his cadres in the hamlets are as hidden as before. The general reserve enters Phase II weakened but whole, and the Front enters it with between 10,000 and 30,000 of the Republic's carbines³. On Guam the B-52Js hold about 1,400 measured targets in the cell's folders and authority to strike none of them in the North.

Phung Hoang ends the phase with about 140 district centres open, every one behind a settled post, and a method that has reached above the hamlet in one district on the edge of Saigon and in a dozen in the Delta⁴. About 1,100 selected advisers are in the subsectors and battalions, speaking to their counterparts without interpreters; the rest of the field posts are still held on the old tour. The Front has begun to move its district committees out of the held belt, which costs it the villages' daily obedience and gains it the safety of the contested edge.

By the end of July 1965 the board has filled about 70 of the army's roughly 190 manoeuvre battalion commands and relieved its first nine commanders; the rest are still held by men the generals put there, and about a third of all battalions are still commanded by captains, because the army is short of majors and the career-course gate makes none faster⁵. The companies are led almost everywhere by the classes of 1957–63. The generals are the generals of 1963, and every one of them has learned that the board can be bargained with and cannot be ignored.

The Directorate ends the phase with its plants at about half their capacity and the domestic share four months old; about 5,000 PF radios, 6,000 hamlet radios and 600,000 dry cells have gone to the held belt, and the Front's mines in Long An have Go Vap batteries in them⁶. Route 1 on the coast has been reopened after the worst flood in memory, and the Front has an industrial working class in Bien Hoa to organise.

The army that enters Phase II has trained every private it has enlisted for eight years, and every territorial; it has kept about 2,000–3,000 of its best sergeants at the training centres to do it, in the two years it could least spare them, and the Muster Service has caught the centres that sold the course short. The general reserve was broken at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai and came back from both with more of its men than on any course before this one; the battalions are steadier than history's by a band, though the enemy still chooses where they fight⁷.

The NCO corps that enters Phase II has been schooled for its grades for eight years, regular and territorial alike, and about 1,300–2,500 of its best sergeants are teaching at Nha Trang, the division schools and the territorial centres, on top of the drill sergeants at Quang Trung⁸. The 4th Marine Battalion at Binh Gia and the 7th Airborne at Dong Xoai were broken and came back with more of their men than on either earlier course, because their sergeants took command when their officers fell. The enemy has the academy's leader's manual and has begun to teach its local forces the ARVN platoon's routine.

The combined command ends the phase as a channel, not yet a command. It survived Khanh's coup by passing every order through his office, and it learned in its first month that operational control means what the junta of the day allows. Seoul and Canberra have consented on conditions: a Korean countersignature on every order to a Korean formation, and an Australian casualty estimate sent to Canberra. The task force ends the phase about 1,100 strong, with one campaign that found nothing for two months and then broke the Can Giuoc security section from one notebook⁹. The Hoc Mon committee that STILL WATER drove out governs from Cu Chi, and the task force's III Corps task group has its name.

The North ends the phase without the fixed economy it began 1965 with. Its fuel is in drums, its power in village diesels, its bridges are pontoons by night, its fighters are in China, and four SA-2 battalions rotate among about twenty sites that the Js strike as they are built. About 300,000–400,000 of its people are already repairing and carrying full time, a year early, and the Politburo has held three divisions at home against a landing that is not coming¹⁰. The flow south is untouched, and the American decision of July is history's.

MACV-JSOC ends the phase four months old and Delta five, with 31 raids in the Saigon belt and the upper Delta, nine of them reaching a cadre the file had listed, and one operator dead at a doorway in Can Giuoc. Its one finished operation is NIGHT HERON, which took six of the eleven men of the Long An province committee at a sampan mooring with the province finance section's ledgers, and cut the Front's collections in three districts to about a third of the previous year's by December¹¹. The partnered cordon has been tried twice and abandoned, because a Ranger company told the hamlet what was coming and the battalion had to be told the night before. The unit has learned the country and has not yet learned what it will learn in Dinh Tuong: that the men it hunts can simply move, and that the price of its arrival is paid in the enemy's walking time.

The night over the posts changed in this phase and the war did not change with it. From January 1964 sixty-four AC-130J Ghostriders flew over the South every night, and by the summer of 1965 the Front had stopped assaulting the posts within their net on clear nights, moved its attacks into the rain, onto the posts beyond the net and into the mortar and the mine, and begun to fight from inside the hamlets. Nam Dong and Dong Xoai cost fewer lives at night and the same by day¹².

### New: The gunship wing's first season
*8 Jan – 30 Jun 1964 · Bien Hoa, Nha Trang and Da Nang air bases; the posts of Long An, Dinh Tuong, Kien Hoa and Vinh Long Provinces · EV015-1*

*Initiative: allied*

The 14th Air Commando Wing (Gunship) flew its first combat sortie on the night of 8–9 January 1964, a week after its 64 AC-130J Ghostriders were placed under the 2nd Air Division at Tan Son Nhut. The rules were Farm Gate's: an American combat aircraft over the South flew with a Vietnamese aboard, in support of the RVNAF, and fired only with the province chief's clearance. Each Ghostrider carried a VNAF observer from the 1st Air Division, who spoke to the province and sector nets, and the wing's crews learned in their first week that the observer was not a formality but the only man aboard who could tell a Popular Forces platoon from the men attacking it¹².

The first engagement was over Kien Hoa. At 0140 on 9 January the PF post at Phu Tuc, on the Ham Luong north of Truc Giang, called the district on its PRC-10 that a company was in the coconut groves on its eastern side and that its wire was being cut. The district relayed the call to the sector, the sector to the air support operations centre at Can Tho, and Can Tho to Ghostrider 41, on station over the Mekong 30 nautical miles north. The aircraft was over Phu Tuc at 0209. Its infrared turret showed about sixty men in two lines among the palms 150–250 metres from the post's eastern wall and a mortar team of four in a ditch beyond them. The province chief's clearance came at 0221. The 105mm put eighteen rounds on the two lines and the mortar ditch by 0240, and the 30mm took the men who ran toward the river. The company of the Ben Tre provincial battalion left 21 dead on the eastern side; the post lost two wounded. The district reported 70 enemy killed. The video, reviewed at Tan Son Nhut the next day, showed between 18 and 25, and it was the video's figure that went to MACV¹².

Through the spring the wing flew about 400–600 sorties a month in III and IV Corps and fewer in I and II Corps, and answered about 120–180 calls a month from posts under attack. Two lessons came fast. The first was that the gunship was worth as much as the radio that called it: posts with a set on the district net were answered, and posts without one were found burning. The second was clearance. In January the median wait for a province chief's approval was about 35 minutes, and on bad nights over an hour; in the middle of a contested district the post was often overrun while the aircraft circled with its guns trained. In July this headquarters, with the Joint General Staff, delegated clearance for fire within 300 metres of a post under attack to the district chief, and the median wait fell to about 12 minutes¹². The price of that rule was paid later, in hamlets beside the posts.

The Front's answer came in March, and it was the first of many. COSVN's Military Affairs Committee, from reports of its Delta regions, issued a directive to the regional commands on "the aircraft that sees in the dark": no assault on a post with a radio on clear nights within reach of the airfields; attacks on posts in rain, on posts far from the airfields, and on posts that could not call; and the assault made fast, to be over the wall before the aircraft came. The directive credited the aircraft with radar it did not have, and through the north-east monsoon of 1964–65 the provincial units of the coast did not exploit the cloud as they could have. By the end of June 1964, in the held belt of Long An and Dinh Tuong, assaults on posts with radios on clear nights had nearly stopped, and the Front's local companies had turned to the mortar from 300 metres, the mine on the dike and the hamlet official killed by day¹².

### Changed: The camps, the bases and the towns: Nam Dong, Bien Hoa and Song Be
*6 Jul 1964 – 12 May 1965 · Nam Dong CIDG camp west of Da Nang; Bien Hoa air base; Song Be and Phuoc Binh, Phuoc Long Province · EVCP01-3*

*Initiative: enemy*

Three attacks are told together because they showed one thing three ways: the enemy chose the night and the target, and what held was whatever was already inside the wire.

At 02:30 on 6 July 1964 about two battalions of VC and PAVN, some 800–900 men, attacked the CIDG camp at Nam Dong near the Laotian border, held by Special Forces Detachment A-726 under Captain Roger H. C. Donlon with an Australian warrant officer, 311 Montagnard strikers, 50 Nungs and seven Vietnamese Special Forces. The outer perimeter was penetrated and many strikers deserted or went over; the inner perimeter, held by the Americans and the Nungs, survived five hours of close fighting until the attackers withdrew at dawn. Two Americans and the Australian were killed, 58 strikers and Nungs died, more than 100 strikers defected, and 55–62 attackers' bodies lay inside the wire; Donlon became the first American awarded the Medal of Honor in Vietnam¹³. The strikers carried the weapons they had always carried, because the rearmament did not reach the CIDG.

On the night of 31 October–1 November, two days before the American election, a VC mortar team fired on Bien Hoa air base for about thirty minutes, destroying five of the B-57Bs parked wingtip to wingtip there since the Tonkin crisis and destroying or damaging as many as 30 aircraft in all; four Americans were killed and 72 people wounded, and the attackers escaped¹⁴. In this war an 81mm round burst on the revetment of the U-2S that was in maintenance that night and holed its left wing, fuel cells and forward equipment bay. It was out of service from 1 November to 20 December, and the daily deep look over the panhandle, where the dry season's first trucks were moving, lapsed to twice a week¹⁵. I asked for and got a covered shelter for each U-2S, built by the Seabees by February 1965, and a Regional Forces company for the hamlets on the base's approaches¹⁶. Johnson declined a reprisal on the eve of the election, and the question of who would guard the bases brought the first American combat troops ashore four months later¹⁷.

On 10–11 May 1965 B-2 Front forces, the 763rd Regiment with the 840th Battalion or elements of the 271st–273rd Regiments, attacked Song Be, the capital of Phuoc Long, and the district town of Phuoc Binh. The 36th Ranger Battalion, about 150 territorials and about three dozen American advisers of Detachment B-34 held the town with the gunships of the 197th Aviation Company, and a relieving Ranger battalion arrived by midday on 11 May. The ARVN lost 58 killed, 96 wounded and 83 missing, five Americans were killed and a B-57 was lost; MACV's estimate of up to 1,000 enemy killed and wounded is of the kind A13 warns against¹⁸. The Rangers had carried the M4A1 and the M249 since February 1964. I do not adjust the losses, most of which were taken in the first hour to mortars, recoilless rifles and sappers inside the wire, where the squad weapons counted for little¹⁹.

In this war a fourth thing stood over each of the three nights, and it changed what was inside the wire at Nam Dong and nothing at Song Be. At Nam Dong a Ghostrider of the 16th Squadron from Da Nang, 50 kilometres away, was over the camp at 0305, thirty-five minutes after the first mortar rounds, in clear sky. The attackers who had broken through the outer perimeter were by then among the strikers' huts and could not be fired on, but the assault companies still forming in the treeline to the west and the mortar positions on the hill to the north could, and the 105mm and 30mm worked them for two and a half hours, until the attack broke off at about 0530 rather than at dawn. Donlon's inner perimeter held as it held historically. I put the strikers' and Nungs' dead at about 40 rather than 58, the two Americans and the Australian killed as historically because they fell in the first hour, and the attackers' dead at about 90–120, the video counting about 70 in the treeline. At Bien Hoa on 1 November the mortar team's rounds fell among the gunships as well as the B-57s: two Ghostriders of the 4th Squadron were hit on the ramp, one destroyed by fire and one out of service for six weeks, and from that night this headquarters asked for, and in March 1965 received with the Marines' and the Koreans' arrival, a ground force to hold the approaches to every gunship base. At Song Be the Ghostriders were over the town from 0115 on 11 May and fired through the night, but the losses had been taken in the first hour inside the wire, to mortars, recoilless rifles and sappers already among the defenders, where no aircraft could fire; the gunships broke the second assault at about 0400 and covered the Ranger battalion's landing at first light, and I do not adjust the allied losses¹².

### New: The night under the cloud at Hoai Nhon
*14–15 Dec 1964 · The PF post at Tam Quan and the district town of Hoai Nhon, Binh Dinh Province; Qui Nhon airfield · EV015-2*

*Initiative: enemy*

The night that ended the gunship's work below the cloud came in the first north-east monsoon of the war. At 2310 on 14 December the post at Tam Quan, on Route 1 north of Bong Son, called Hoai Nhon district that it was under attack by a company of the 2nd Regiment of the Front's Military Region 5. The cloud base over the coast was about 1,800 feet, with rain. Ghostrider 63 of the 14th Squadron, on station south of Qui Nhon, came north and found nothing on its turrets but the glow of the post's flares through the cloud. Its commander, Major Thomas R. Gaither, took the aircraft down through the overcast to 1,500 feet to see, as two crews of the squadron had done successfully in November¹².

He found the attack at once and it found him. The company had two 12.7mm machine guns sited on the paddy dikes south of the post, and they opened on the aircraft's first turn. The Ghostrider fired for about six minutes and broke the assault on the southern wall; in those minutes it took about thirty rounds of 12.7mm through the left wing and the fuel tanks, lost an engine and a hydraulic system, and was flown back to Qui Nhon on three engines with a fire in the wing that the fuel-tank protection kept from spreading. Two crewmen were wounded. The post at Tam Quan held until 0400, when the attack was renewed in the rain with no aircraft overhead, and fell; nineteen of its thirty men were killed or taken¹².

On 16 December the wing forbade attacks below 3,500 feet. From then on, on monsoon nights over the coast, the Ghostrider could give the posts of Binh Dinh, Quang Ngai and Quang Nam nothing but a GPS weapon on a coordinate the posts could not give it, and the Front's provincial units, which had believed since March that the aircraft saw through cloud, learned over the winter that it did not¹². It was the provision's limit (D14), found in a night.

### Changed: The battle of Dong Xoai
*9–13 Jun 1965 · Dong Xoai district town and CIDG camp, Phuoc Long Province · EV000-18*

*Initiative: enemy*

Late on 9 June 1965 the VC 272nd Regiment, with a battalion of the 273rd, a 75mm recoilless rifle company, an 82mm mortar company, a flamethrower company and anti-aircraft machine guns, attacked the district headquarters and CIDG camp at Dong Xoai; the 271st Regiment lay in reserve in the Thuan Loi rubber plantation. The camp was held by Special Forces Detachment A-342, nine men of Navy Seabee Team 1104, three CIDG companies, the 111th Regional Force Company and militia, with six armoured cars and two 105mm howitzers. The CIDG companies and the militia carried the carbines and Garands they had always carried, because the rearmament did not reach them; the 111th RF Company and the Americans carried M4A1s. The camp was largely overrun during the night, as it was historically, from the CIDG sectors inward, and the survivors held out in the district headquarters, where the 111th Company had fallen back with its carbines, until helicopters of the 118th Aviation Company lifted them out. On 10 June the 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment (ARVN 5th Division), was landed at Thuan Loi and overrun, losing about half its men against nearly all of them historically³; the 52nd Ranger Battalion retook the town; on 11 June the 7th Airborne Battalion arrived with about 470 men, and on 12 June the 271st ambushed it in the rubber²⁰.

The Airborne fight on 12 June is the clearest measure in this war of what the squad weapons could and could not do. Historically about 150 of the 470 came back. On this course the battalion's lead company was lost in the opening fire as it was historically, but the three companies behind it each turned their squad guns into the trees and held, and about 270 men fought their way to the landing zone at Thuan Loi over the afternoon, bringing about 60 wounded. The 271st had chosen the place, the hour and the range, and it won; the Airborne battalion was broken, though not wiped out³. The 145th Aviation Battalion committed every aircraft it had²⁰.

I put the allied losses at about 300 South Vietnamese killed, 210 wounded and 150 missing, and 18 Americans killed as historically, against 416 killed, 174 wounded and 233 missing on the historical course; about 300 civilians were killed and 2,500 made refugees, as historically. More than 300 VC bodies were found historically; I put the figure here at about 400, with the same scepticism about the allied estimate of 625 more. Second Lieutenant Charles Q. Williams and Construction Mechanic Third Class Marvin G. Shields received the Medal of Honor, Shields posthumously, the only Seabee so honoured. On 13 June Westmoreland committed the 1st Battalion, 503rd Infantry of the 173rd Airborne Brigade to Phuoc Vinh, the first commitment of US ground troops to a major battle; the VC had already gone, and the battalion returned on 18 June without contact²⁰. After Dong Xoai the ARVN in III Corps had about two reserve battalions left, against one historically³. That was not enough to change Westmoreland's request of 7 June, which rested on the PAVN regiments entering the Highlands as much as on the battalions lost, and it did not change the answer.

At Dong Xoai the board had not yet reached the 5th Division. The 1st Battalion, 7th Regiment was landed at Thuan Loi on 10 June on a division plan that put it on an open landing zone beside the rubber where the 271st was known to be waiting, under a battalion commander appointed by the division in 1962. The board reviewed the landing in July on its own motion, under the thirty-day rule, and in August relieved the battalion commander and the division operations officer who had written the plan, the first reliefs for cause in the ARVN's history that were not punishments for political disloyalty⁵. The 5th Division's commander was untouched, and remained so, because he had been appointed before the ranked list existed. The night at the camp and the 7th Airborne's fight on 12 June went as told above²⁰.

The basic course changed Dong Xoai at its edges and not at its centre. The CIDG companies, which the course did not reach, broke first, as they had historically and in this war before it. The 111th RF Company, which had taken the territorial course as a company in 1961, fell back to the district headquarters in order and carried its wounded with it; the 1st Battalion, 7th Regiment, whose privates had all been through Quang Trung, was still landed on the plan its division wrote, on the open zone beside the rubber, and still lost about half its men, because no private's training reaches a landing zone chosen for him. The difference was in the evening of 12 June, when the 7th Airborne's survivors came into Thuan Loi: of about 60 wounded they brought out, about 50 were alive the next morning, with tourniquets put on in the rubber by men who had never been taught first aid on the historical course and were taught it in basic here. I put the allied killed at about 270 rather than about 300, a judgment on the wounded who lived and the companies that held, and I do not adjust the enemy's losses⁷.

The sergeants changed Dong Xoai at the same edges. The 111th RF Company had passed the territorial courses for every NCO grade, and its platoon sergeants, not its officers, took it back to the district headquarters in order, a platoon at a time, while the CIDG companies, whose leaders the grant did not reach, broke around it. On 12 June the 7th Airborne's three surviving companies were held together, after their captains were hit, by first sergeants and acting squad leaders who had all passed the leader's course, and about 290 men reached Thuan Loi rather than about 270. The 1st Battalion, 7th Regiment, was still landed on the open zone beside the rubber, on the division's plan, and no sergeant could change that. I put the allied killed at about 255 rather than about 270⁸.

The gunships changed the night at Dong Xoai and not the two days after it. Three Ghostriders of the 4th Squadron from Bien Hoa, 100 kilometres south, were over the camp from about 0010 on 10 June, in broken cloud with showers that let them see the ground about half the time. The 272nd's first assault had already carried the CIDG sectors, and the gunships could not fire into the camp; but the regiment's second wave, two battalions forming in the open between the rubber and the district headquarters' wire at about 0200, was found on the infrared turrets and broken by the 105mm and 30mm before it reached the headquarters, and the 75mm recoilless rifles firing on the headquarters from the edge of the rubber were silenced one by one through the rest of the night. The regiment's anti-aircraft machine guns fired on the aircraft all night and hit one, without bringing it down. The 111th RF Company and the Americans in the district headquarters held until the helicopters came, as they did, and I judge that fewer of them were killed in the night, about 15–25 fewer. The landing of the 1st Battalion, 7th Regiment at Thuan Loi on 10 June and the 7th Airborne's fight in the rubber on 12 June were daylight fights the gunships did not touch, and they went as told above. I put the allied killed at about 230–240 rather than about 255, and the enemy's dead at about 450–500, with the caution that applies to every count made at night¹².

## Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 military personnel in Vietnam and has lost 9,378 of them killed by hostile action in the year²¹. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December²², and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December. The enemy order of battle is in dispute: MACV counts about 300,000 communist personnel, the CIA up to 430,000²³, and the disagreement turns on whether the guerrillas and the political infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all.

On 21 November Westmoreland tells the National Press Club that the enemy is "unable to mount a major offensive" and that "the end begins to come into view"²³. The administration's progress campaign of the autumn rests on the body count, the Hamlet Evaluation System and the claim that the crossover point is near. McNamara, who has lost confidence in the war, has announced his departure for the World Bank, and Johnson's offer at San Antonio on 29 September, to stop the bombing in exchange for prompt and productive talks, has been rejected by Hanoi. In Saigon there is, for the first time since 1963, an elected government under Thieu, and in the countryside CORDS has begun to organize the territorial war, from a less low base than history's. About 820,000 hectares have been titled to about 640,000 families, rent has ended in law and largely in fact wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general. The infrastructure of the Front is smaller in the Delta than on the historical course, and its tax take lower, but it is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, and those hamlets are still most of the contested countryside¹.

In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.

In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts by the end of 1967, and the arrest count has fallen because there is little left there to arrest². The National Police numbers about 80,000, the chiefs have mostly held their districts for two or three years, and the Front's legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less.

The enemy's external supply is measured: the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count, the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what the South's forces need from the North¹⁶. That knowledge is honest from 1965 rather than from 1970, and it has not changed the rules, the bombing or the strategy. Its main effect on Washington has been to deliver bad news early.

The RVNAF enters 1968 with the rifles it has carried for four years and a Regional Force that the corps commanders want for their own operations, bound since 1967 by the rule that keeps it in its provinces. The American army has had no rifle crisis and no inquiry, and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights; it is the same army in every other respect, fighting the same battles on the enemy's terms.

The bombers have learned two things in two years: that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle. The second lesson is the one the headquarters remembers going into 1968.

Phung Hoang has a centre in every district and an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, about one in five of them members of district or village committees, and the Front's district administration in the held belt now governs from the contested edge by courier. The word Phoenix has been a press story since March 1967. About 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps; the American battalions have changed over once or twice each as units, have fought better in the contacts they were granted, and have learned at Dien Ban to keep their reliefs off the dark of the moon. The staggered six-week overlap that followed raised the peak American strength in theater by about 15,000–25,000 men, which the expansion battalions of 1967 waited for, so that the enemy's tactic against the relief was paid for in American spaces rather than American dead⁴. None of it has changed who chooses the battle.

The ARVN ends 1967 with about four in five of its battalions commanded by officers the board chose, on eighteen-month commands, with the captain-led battalion nearly gone and the thirty-day review feared and read; about a third fewer of its battalions have been rendered ineffective in 1966–67 than on the historical course, which no report shows because the enemy declined the fights that would have shown it⁵. The 25th Division has a commander from the list and the corps have the commanders they had. The Military Security Service has its first file on the board's officers as a political factor, and COSVN has had every list the board published.

The factories end 1967 producing what the domestic share buys, with the steelworks short of power and the arsenal short of its gunners' trust after Phu Cat. Every post of the held belt has a radio, the Front attacks those that can call about a third less often than those that cannot, and where the guns can reach the posts the first call is for fire⁶. The posts hold themselves better than the hamlets around them.

The ARVN ends 1967 trained to the man; training alone would have left it as short of squad leaders as history's, and what filled most of the empty slots was the NCO schooling described below; its battalions have lost about a tenth to a sixth fewer men in the ambushes the enemy still lays, beyond what the rifles and the officers saved, and about one in eight fewer battalions has been broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms alone would have left. The drill-sergeant corps has begun to return about 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year to the battalions⁷. In the lowlands of Quang Nam and Quang Ngai the mine has replaced the firefight as the enemy's way of killing Americans, and in the districts around Saigon the Front's guerrilla squads are drilled by men the Republic trained.

The ARVN ends 1967 with its squads and platoons led by schooled men: about two in three of the slots the field commissions emptied are held by corporals first class who passed the leader's course, and the squads of the 7th Division held their base of fire at Hau My when their officers fell. I judge that about one in six to one in five fewer ARVN battalions were broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms and the basic course alone would have left, and that the posts of the Delta lost about a tenth to a fifth fewer to night attack than the radio and the trained platoon had already saved⁸. None of it shows in a return: the enemy attacked less what kept its routine. American sergeants pass the Basic Leader Course at Bien Hoa or wait for it, and the waiver of 1966 has become a ninety-day deferral.

The combined command ends 1967 with one corps area under a Vietnamese commander and three under American deputies who in practice run them, a quarterly plan the corps commanders execute at their own speed, and a two-layer plan that protects its operations and insults its Vietnamese staff. The task force has broken the Front's district government of the Saigon belt from its edge: the Hoc Mon committee and the region's finance section govern from the Ho Bo woods, and the region's collections from the posted villages are about an eighth of 1964's⁹. On the II Corps coast it has a list it abandoned and a story the Front still tells.

Over the North the phase ends with the campaign the theater asked for and the result it predicted. In October 1966 this command reported that the northern campaign was destroying everything in the North that could be destroyed and that the North's war in the South needed none of it, and the barrier began from that report. The air defence that history's gradualism let the North build under sanctuary was built instead under fire and from China: about 120 MiGs fighting from Chinese fields, and SA-2 battalions three sites to a launcher. About 40–90 fewer American aircraft were lost over the North in 1966–67 than historically, and the Stennis hearings on the restrictions were never held¹⁰.

Delta ends the phase with its rate found and its limit found with it. Thirty-eight raids a month in 1966 and 44 in 1967, 297 listed cadre at district level or above in the two years, 61 of them province or region committee members, and nine finance sections taken with their ledgers; four in five of the raids in III and IV Corps, because that is where the file is. Ninety-four reconnaissance missions into the Laotian panhandle under the ambassador's limits produced the first measured coordinates under canopy in this war and changed what arrives in the South by one to four points, inside the width the phase already holds¹¹. Fourteen operators are dead, four missing near the Ban Laboy ford, fifty-one wounded, and about a quarter of the men in the assault troops were selected after the war began, because the unit was committed whole and has nowhere to rotate to. And in the upper Delta the enemy has answered the whole provision with three sentences in a COSVN circular: senior cadre do not sleep twice in a hamlet, committees meet across the border, couriers carry nothing written. The committees of Dinh Tuong now govern their districts from Memot at two months' remove, their collections at about a sixth of 1964's, and the raid yield that measures this success is falling.

The gunships end 1967 with the clear night over the posts of the held belt taken from the Front, the monsoon night on the coast still its own, a hunter on every truck track in the panhandle that tonnage arriving barely notices, and the first Vietnamese gunship squadron flying. The ambush of the relief on the canal road is answered from the air.

### Changed: Plei Me and the Ia Drang
*19 Oct – 18 Nov 1965 · Plei Me CIDG camp and the Ia Drang valley below the Chu Pong massif, Pleiku Province · EV000-23*

*Initiative: enemy*

On 19 October 1965 the PAVN B3 Front under Major General Chu Huy Man attacked the Special Forces camp at Plei Me, south of Pleiku, and the next day ambushed the ARVN relief column; the relief reached the camp at dusk on 25 October and the PAVN withdrew west towards the Chu Pong massif on the Cambodian border. The 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile), newly arrived, was turned loose in pursuit. On 14 November the 1st Battalion, 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Harold G. Moore air-assaulted into Landing Zone X-Ray at the foot of the Chu Pong, into the assembly area of the 66th Regiment. For three days the 7th and 9th Battalions of the 66th, with elements of the 33rd, assaulted a perimeter held with the help of the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Robert Tully, massed tube artillery, tactical air and, from 15 November, B-52s striking about 7 km to the west, the first tactical use of the bombers, in five missions and 96 sorties over the campaign. The troopers carried M4A1s, with two M249s in each squad and an M110A2 marksman in most, where historically they carried the M16 and had the M60 at platoon; the perimeter held as it held historically, and I put American losses at X-Ray at about 70 killed and 115 wounded against 79 and 121³. Moore's count of PAVN dead, 634 after his own reduction, and the estimate of 1,215 remain the figures of record and the same caution applies to them²⁴.

On 17 November the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Robert McDade, marching overland to Landing Zone Albany, was ambushed in column in tall grass by the 8th Battalion, 66th Regiment and the 1st Battalion, 33rd Regiment. The PAVN, following Colonel Nguyen Huu An's order to "grab them by the belt", fought inside the column where American artillery and air could not reach them, for about sixteen hours. This is the kind of fight the squad gun was built for, and it helped less than it should have. Two belt-fed guns in every squad meant that the platoons which kept their cohesion, Alpha Company's and the battalion command group's at the head of the column, formed a perimeter in the clump of trees at Albany within minutes and held it all afternoon; but the companies strung out behind in the grass were broken into knots of men who could not see each other at 20 metres, and a machine gun is no use to a squad that cannot find its targets or its friends. The battalion lost about 125 killed, 130 wounded and 4 missing, against 155 killed, 124 wounded and 4 missing on the historical course, still the worst American loss of a single day so far. Over the campaign the United States counted about 205 dead, against 237 historically, and claimed a kill ratio of about ten to one; a PAVN report of 1966 gives 559 killed and 669 wounded³. Both sides inflated the other's losses²⁴.

Both commands judged the Ia Drang a success, and each drew the lesson that confirmed its strategy: Westmoreland that airmobile forces with heavy fire support could destroy PAVN regulars at a favourable rate; the PAVN that by closing to close quarters and choosing when to fight they could neutralize American firepower and withdraw across the Cambodian border to rebuild²⁴. The B3 Front's after-action study added one sentence that the historical one did not need: that the American squads now carried "a light machine gun in every cell", and that the belt-grabbing assault must therefore be made from closer still, at night, or not at all³. McNamara, visiting after the battle, advised the President at the end of November that even a doubling of US forces in 1966 might produce only a military stalemate at a higher level.

The officer education changed Albany in the companies and not in the column's order. Moore and McDade had been commissioned long before 1957 and the decision to march overland in column through the grass was McDade's; but the company commanders of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry were captains of the classes of 1959–62, and they had been through the branch course and the career course, which taught the movement to contact in close country as a drill. Two of them put flank security out into the grass on their own authority when the column halted at about midday, and their companies were the ones whose men were found in perimeters rather than in knots; two did not, because the column was moving and the battalion had given no order. I put the battalion's loss at about 105–115 killed rather than about 125, a judgment on two companies' conduct that I hold loosely, and the campaign's American dead at about 190⁵. It remains the worst American loss of a single day so far.

The basic course changed Albany in the night after the ambush, which is where the battalion lost men it need not have lost. The troopers of the 1st Cavalry Division had all passed the Army's ten-week course of the 2026 programme, and every one of them had been taught in its second week to put a tourniquet on an arm or a leg and to put it on himself if no one else could²⁵. Historically, many of the wounded of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry lay in the grass through the afternoon and night of 17 November, where the medics could not reach them, and a share of those found dead in the morning had died of wounds that a tourniquet would have stopped²⁴²⁶. Here the men in the grass put them on each other and on themselves, in the dark, while the PAVN searched the field. I put the lives this saved at Albany at about eight to twelve, and at X-Ray at two or three, and the campaign's American dead at about 180 rather than about 190. That is the rate this headquarters uses for the whole war, about two to four percent of American killed in action, shown on one night in one battle; it is not larger, and on that night it was not smaller. The PAVN wounded who reached the Chu Pong had no such drill, and the B3 Front's medical returns, captured in 1966, put its dead of wounds after the battle at about one in four of its wounded⁷.

In this war the gunships were over Plei Me from its first night and over X-Ray and Albany through every night of the battle, and they changed the nights and not the days. At Plei Me the 33rd Regiment's assaults of 19–21 October came at night, and Ghostriders of the 14th Squadron from Nha Trang were over the camp within about forty minutes of the first, in clear dry-season air; the regiment's third night assault on the southern wall was broken in the open by the 105mm, and the camp's strikers, who historically held with tactical air and flares, held with fewer dead. The ambush of the ARVN relief column on 23 October was laid by day and went as history's did. At X-Ray two gunships held the night of 14–15 November over Moore's perimeter, and the 7th Battalion, 66th Regiment, which historically probed the perimeter through the night and attacked at 0650, was found forming on the slope of the Chu Pong at about 0400 and taken under fire there; the dawn attack came in thinner and was held. At Albany on the night of 17–18 November the gunship could not fire into the grass where the knots of Americans and PAVN lay among each other, and it did the one thing it could: it lit the field from above with its infrared marker, found the PAVN search parties moving between the knots, and fired on them where the strobes in the troopers' helmets showed them more than 100 metres from any American. I put the lives the gunships saved over the campaign at about 10–20, most of them at Albany that night and at Plei Me, and the campaign's American dead at about 165–170. The B3 Front's study of the campaign added a third sentence to the two it had: that the American aircraft "that sees in the dark" made the night assault on a prepared position as costly as the day assault, and that the belt-grabbing attack must be made under cloud or in the forest or not at all¹².

### New: Operation NIGHT LANTERN
*15 Nov 1965 – 30 Apr 1966 · Can Giuoc and Can Duoc Districts, Long An Province · EV002-4*

*Initiative: allied*
NIGHT LANTERN went back to the districts where the land programme had learned its first lesson. Eighteen months after the Can Giuoc killings, the titles of about 400 families were still held in the district office, because no one could protect the families who kept them. Long An had been given a province chief from the first list in June 1964, Lieutenant Colonel Ha Thuc Lan, an engineer officer who had placed third in the country in the examination, and Can Giuoc a district chief from the second, Major Le Cong Phuong, who had grown up in Can Duoc. In September 1965 they proposed to the American province adviser an operation built not around a regiment but around the settled post, the census and night check and the target folder, in the 14 villages of the two districts between Route 5 and the Vam Co².

The forces were Long An's own: eight Regional Forces companies, 26 Popular Forces platoons raised in the villages themselves, two Police Field Force companies of about 150 men each with M1 and M2 carbines, M1918A2 automatic rifles and 60mm mortars, 140 rural constables for the 14 posts, the province Special Branch section of about 45, and four census teams. Fire support was two M101 105mm howitzers at Can Giuoc and an AC-130J Ghostrider of the USAF 4th Air Commando Squadron on call at night from Bien Hoa; lift was the RF's sampans, two LCVPs of the River Assault Group at Nha Be, and UH-1B helicopters when III Corps would release them. The rule was Lan's: no post settled until its PF platoon slept in the same hamlet and a reaction force could reach it by water within the hour, and no arrest without three sources².

The posts went in from 15 November, one village at a time, working out from Can Giuoc town along the canals. The turn came in two steps. On the night of 19 January 1966 two companies of the 506th Local Force Battalion attacked the new post at Phuoc Lai, the village where the killings of June 1964 had begun. The PF platoon and the ten constables held the post and the hamlet behind it for three hours; an RF company came down the canal in sampans and reached the post at 01:40, and the Ghostrider kept the attackers off the paddy until it arrived. The 506th left 38 dead and 14 weapons; the defenders lost 9 killed, 3 of them constables. On 4 February a night check in Long Huu found a young man whose card had been made for someone two years older; his booklet did not match the house, and within a week the courier route he served had led the Special Branch to the chief of the Can Giuoc district committee's security section, arrested on 11 February with his files². The Can Giuoc DIOCC, open since August 1964 in the Special Branch's office beside the district chief's, took the files apart in nine days: the section chief's notebook listed the committee's courier stations by the names of the families who kept them, and the census matched 17 of the 22 to households and three to households that had been registered under false names in 1965. On the night of 24–25 February the Long An PRU and a Police Field Force platoon, in sampans with an RF company holding the canal behind them, took the district committee's deputy secretary and its finance chief in a hamlet of Phuoc Vinh Dong at the edge of the Rung Sat, where the committee had moved in January believing itself beyond the posts⁴. Neither man fired. The deputy secretary rallied in April and spent the rest of the year with the province centre, drawing the chart of the Long An province committee above him.

By 30 April all 14 posts were settled and held. The Special Branch had arrested 212 people on three-source evidence, of whom the magistrates released 71, and 64 cadres and guerrillas had rallied to the police posts, which they found easier to approach than an army camp. What was left of the district committee, five of its eleven members, moved deeper into the Rung Sat and visited its villages instead of living in them, and the Can Giuoc tax ledger captured in June showed collections for the first quarter of 1966 at about a third of the same quarter of 1965. The about 400 titles held since 1964 were handed to their families in April, in their hamlets². NIGHT LANTERN cost 31 RF, PF and police dead. It was the first operation in the war in which the province chief, the police and the land programme acted as one district government, and it did in six months what no battalion sweep of Long An had done in six years.

The American who saw the whole of it was Captain Whitcomb, the Can Giuoc subsector adviser, whose eighteen months ran from October 1964 to April 1966 and so spanned the killings' aftermath, the settling of the posts and the operation itself; his successor arrived on 1 March and they worked the district together for six weeks. Whitcomb's report of 30 April said three things this headquarters quoted to Washington: that the committee's arrest, not the battalion's sweep, was what broke the tax; that the Commission's sample of NIGHT LANTERN's 212 arrests had found 9 unsupported, all made in the first fortnight before the centre's charts were complete; and that the families who received their titles in April had asked him, not the district chief, whether the arrests would last⁴.

### New: Operation STEADY COUNT
*6 Dec 1965 – 30 Apr 1966 · Mu Gia and Ban Karai passes; Routes 23, 911 and 912 south to Tchepone; the Laotian panhandle · EV003-3*

*Initiative: allied*
STEADY COUNT was the first dry season of the panhandle watch, and it was named for what it did best. On 6 December 1965, the day Tiger Hound opened its strikes in the southern panhandle, the Global Hawk orbit moved from the II Corps coast to a racetrack over the Mekong side of the Laotian panhandle west of Tchepone, outside the guns and beyond the reach of anything the North could fly. From 60,000 feet its radar watched the roads that Group 559 had cut through the Annamite Chain that year: Route 23 south from the Mu Gia pass, Routes 911 and 912 from Ban Karai, and the fords and truck parks along the Xe Bang Fai and the Xe Banghiang down to Tchepone and Route 9¹⁵. The northeast monsoon gave Laos its dry season, and low cloud lay on the passes most mornings in January; the radar saw through it.

The engagement ran through three headquarters, and its weakness was in the joints. A track of six or more vehicles moving south at night went from the exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut to the 2nd Air Division's control centre, from 1 April the Seventh Air Force's, and to the airborne command post, which passed it to whatever was in the air: A-1E Skyraiders of the 602nd Air Commando Squadron, B-57Bs, F-100Ds and F-105Ds on armed reconnaissance, and from the first night the AC-130J Ghostriders of the 17th Air Commando Squadron from Ubon, which flew to the tracks themselves¹². Strikes in Laos needed the rules approved by Ambassador William Sullivan in Vientiane, which allowed armed reconnaissance on the motorable roads. Of about 1,900 tracks passed in the five months, aircraft reached about one in six within forty minutes, found and attacked about one in ten, and destroyed or damaged trucks in about one in twenty. The pilots claimed about 560 trucks destroyed; the cell's own count, from tracks that stopped and did not move again and from the U-2S's radar imagery the next day, was about 210. Nine US aircraft were lost over the panhandle in STEADY COUNT's sectors, most of them to 37mm guns that Group 559 moved to the passes from January; seven crewmen were killed or missing¹⁶. The drivers, porters and road troops killed are unknown, and any figure for them would be invented.

What the counts showed was the war's arithmetic. Southbound truck movements through Mu Gia rose from about 20 a night in December to about 120 a night at the peak in March, and the radar measured what came out at the southern end, on the roads toward Route 9 and the A Shau. On 12 April 1966 B-52s struck the Mu Gia pass for the first time; the orbit watched the first trucks move through the craters about twenty hours later. By February the drivers had learned the orbit's habits: traffic fell by half on the nights when the aircraft was late on station and rose in the hours of its changeover, and the road troops began to trellis the open stretches with bamboo and living trees. MACV J-2 estimated, from the tracks, that about 70–90 tons a day reached the South through the panhandle at the dry season's peak, and that this was more than the forces in the South required from the North¹⁶. It was the first time any headquarters had counted the Trail rather than estimating it, and the count said that the bombing raised the toll on the transit without lowering what arrived.

### New: Operation NIGHT LEDGER: the gunships on the panhandle's tracks
*6 Dec 1965 – 30 Apr 1967 · The Laotian panhandle from the Mu Gia pass to Tchepone and the Ban Laboy ford; Ubon Royal Thai Air Force Base; the exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut · EV015-3*

*Initiative: allied*

The Thai government agreed in October 1965 to base a gunship squadron at Ubon, at the price of an increase in American aid and on the condition that nothing be said of it, and the 17th Air Commando Squadron's sixteen Ghostriders moved there from Nha Trang in November. They flew their first armed reconnaissance over the panhandle on the night of 6 December, the night STEADY COUNT began. In this war the operation had a name of its own: NIGHT LEDGER, because from its first week every engagement was recorded on the gunship's video and counted against the radar's tracks in the same cell at Tan Son Nhut¹².

The method was the hand-off the radar had needed. A Global Hawk track of six or more vehicles moving south was passed by satellite link to the airborne command post and from it to the nearest Ghostrider, which flew to the track, found the convoy on its infrared turret at 10–20 kilometres, and engaged it from about 12,000–15,000 feet with Griffins on the lead and rear trucks and the 105mm on the rest. In the first dry season the squadron flew about 8–10 sorties a night and engaged about one track in three within twenty minutes of its passing, against the one in six that the strike force had reached in forty minutes. The video counted about 1,100–1,500 trucks destroyed or disabled from December 1965 to April 1966; the crews claimed about 2,600¹².

Group 559 answered within the season. By February 1966 the convoys on Routes 912 and 23 moved at intervals of five to ten minutes rather than in columns, the truck parks went under the canopy, and two battalions of 37mm guns were moved from the North to the crossings at Ban Laboy and the Xe Bang Fai, about a year earlier than history placed them. Over the wet season the PAVN built bypasses under the trees, and by the dry season of 1966–67 a third of the southbound movements the radar counted ran on roads the canopy closed over, where the gunships could not see them. The 57mm batteries came in the autumn. On the night of 2 March 1967 Ghostrider 22, working a convoy at the Ban Laboy ford at 11,000 feet, was hit by a 57mm battery the electronic order of battle had not shown and went down in the hills west of the ford; three of its nine crewmen were picked up the next morning by an HH-3E from Nakhon Phanom, and six were not found¹².

NIGHT LEDGER's honest arithmetic was the radar's. In the dry season of 1966–67 the video counted about 2,000–2,600 trucks destroyed or disabled, perhaps three to four times what the historical gunships could have done at that date had they existed, and the radar's estimate of the net loss to the throughput rose by about two to four points over the season. Tonnage arriving in the South fell by less: the Trail's capacity was several times its requirement, and the trucks the North lost were replaced by Soviet and Chinese deliveries within the year¹².

### New: Operation GOLDEN SHEAF
*10 Jan – 30 Jun 1966 · Phong Dinh and Chuong Thien Provinces, along the Xa No canal from Can Tho to Vi Thanh · EV001-6*

*Initiative: allied*
GOLDEN SHEAF was the first operation of the war planned around the land programme rather than around an enemy unit. Its object was to carry the titling line west from the Bassac along the Xa No canal, the main waterway from Can Tho to Vi Thanh, into about 60 villages of Phong Dinh and Chuong Thien that the government held by day only or not at all, and to leave behind hamlets held at night by their own titled families. IV Corps gave it to the ARVN 21st Division, with its 31st, 32nd and 33rd Regiments, two Ranger battalions, about 40 Regional Forces companies of the two provinces, 24 titling teams and 6 muster teams; the 21st's advisory team and the American province senior advisers at Can Tho and Vi Thanh planned it with the division staff in November and December 1965. Fire support was the division's M101 105mm howitzers moved by LCM-6 along the canal, VNAF A-1H Skyraiders on call, and AC-130J Ghostriders at night over posts under attack; lift was the US Army helicopter companies in IV Corps, UH-1B and UH-1D, about 30 aircraft on the operation's busiest days¹. The dry season set the timing: from January to April the paddies were dry or stubble, the canal and the main arroyos were the only water lines, and troops could move off the dikes; the rains from May slowed every movement after that²⁷.

The method was the land oil-spot at battalion scale. A regiment cleared a block of four to six villages by day in a sweep of about a week, with Rangers on the far side of the block as a stop line; RF companies, one to each two or three hamlets, stayed in the hamlets overnight rather than withdrawing to posts; the titling teams followed about ten days behind, posting parcel numbers rather than names, and the muster teams recruited a Popular Forces platoon in each titled hamlet from the families who had just received their land, issued M1 carbines and AN/PRC-25 radios through the district, and paid them at the parade. A regiment moved to the next block only when the American province adviser and the district chief rated the last one able to hold at night with its RF company and its new platoon¹.

The enemy declined battle. The Front's Phong Dinh and Chuong Thien provincial battalions and the regional main-force battalion this headquarters' order of battle placed west of the Xa No withdrew south-west towards the U Minh forest as the first blocks were entered, leaving local guerrillas, mines on the dikes and snipers at the canal bends²⁸. The one serious engagement came on the night of 22–23 March, when about two companies attacked an RF company and a new PF platoon in a hamlet at kilometre 28 on the canal; the post held for four hours under a Ghostrider and illumination from the howitzers at Phung Hiep, and the attackers withdrew before dawn leaving 31 bodies and 9 weapons; the defenders lost 14 killed. Across the operation the ARVN, RF and PF lost about 214 killed and 640 wounded, more than half to mines and booby traps. The units reported about 690 enemy killed; the muster teams' audit of the reports, the first ever made of a division's body count, accepted 268 by body and weapon and estimated the true figure at 250–350, and recovered 140 weapons in all¹. Of the reported figure, I am confident only that it is too high.

By 30 June about 46,000 hectares had been titled to about 38,000 families in 112 hamlets, and 74 of those hamlets were rated by the district and the province adviser as held at night by their own forces. The other 38 were held by day, and the titles for them stayed in the district office at Phung Hiep and Long My. The operation stopped at the line the Regional and Popular Forces could hold, about 25 kilometres short of Vi Thanh, not at the limit of the titling teams, who were idle for most of June: the bottleneck had moved from the offer to its delivery. In the 74 held hamlets the Front's tax collectors stopped coming, and in the autumn the province recorded the first rice sales through the government's market at Phung Hiep from villages that had never sold there¹. It is the first place in this war where the government's arrival was what F001-17 said it would be: a guarantee rather than a threat, delivered by the government's own troops to people who had something of their own to defend.

### New: The monsoon nights of Binh Dinh
*15 Oct – 31 Dec 1966 · Hoai Nhon, Phu My and Tam Quan Districts, Binh Dinh Province; the posts on Route 1 and the coastal railway from Bong Son to Phu Cat · EV015-4*

*Initiative: enemy*

This is the season that shows where the night war went when the gunship took the clear nights from it. By October 1966 the posts of the Delta and the Saigon belt within the gunship net were seldom assaulted on clear nights, and in the coastal lowlands of II Corps the Front's Military Region 5 had drawn the conclusion its Delta regions had drawn two years earlier. The 2nd Regiment of the PAVN 3rd (Sao Vang) Division and the Binh Dinh provincial battalions, rebuilt after the Bong Son operations of the spring, prepared through September to attack the posts of the coast in the north-east monsoon, on the nights the cloud came down¹².

The monsoon arrived in the third week of October. On the night of 26–27 October, under a cloud base of about 1,200 feet and in heavy rain, three companies attacked three posts on Route 1 between Bong Son and Tam Quan within an hour of each other. All three called Hoai Nhon district on their sets. The Ghostrider on station south of Qui Nhon came north and orbited above the cloud at 5,000 feet, seeing on its infrared turret only the diffused glow of the flares and the fires; its crew, under the wing's rule of December 1964, did not go down. It dropped two GBU-39s on the coordinates the district gave for a mortar position, which the district had read from a 1:50,000 map in the rain, and the bombs fell about 400 metres from where the mortar had been¹². Two of the three posts fell before dawn. The 105mm battery at Bong Son could reach one of them, and fired.

Through November and December the pattern held. The Front attacked the posts of Hoai Nhon, Phu My and Tam Quan on about 18 of the 30 nights the cloud was below 3,000 feet, and on 2 of the 31 nights it was not. Eleven posts and one district police post fell, about as many as the coast lost in history's same months, and the Front took about 300 weapons, most of them M4A1s, and the files of the Phu My police post¹². The Korean Capital Division's posts south of Qui Nhon were attacked on the same nights and held, because each had a 105mm battery within range; the Korean commanders had not trusted the gunships from the first. In the Delta, where the south-west monsoon's cloud is afternoon convection that clears by midnight, the same months saw the fewest attacks on posts of the war so far.

Major General Vinh Loc's II Corps headquarters sent the season's figures to Saigon in January 1967, and they made two cases. The first was for guns: a district battery within reach of every post on the coast, which the Korean posts had shown worked and which the domestic arsenal could feed. The second was for a gunship that could see through cloud. The Spooky IIs promised to the VNAF had arrived on 1 January; their AN/APQ-180 radar could find a post and fire on offsets from it in any weather, and the Joint General Staff, on Vinh Loc's figures, sent the second VNAF squadron to Nha Trang for the coast rather than to Da Nang¹². The coastal posts' night belonged to the weather for two more monsoons.

### New: The Spooky IIs and the 817th's first night
*1 Jan – 31 Dec 1967 · Bien Hoa air base and the Air Training Centre at Nha Trang; Hurlburt Field, Florida; Duc Hue District, Hau Nghia Province · EV015-5*

*Initiative: allied*

Forty-eight AC-130U Spooky IIs arrived at Bien Hoa and Nha Trang from 1 January 1967 and were handed to a Vietnamese Air Force that had no one to fly them. The VNAF formed the 81st Gunship Wing under Lieutenant Colonel Pham Quang Khiem, a C-47 squadron commander who had flown Farm Gate's observer seat in the Ghostriders in 1964 and was among the first VNAF officers through the Air Command and Staff course, and an American training detachment of about 300 under the 14th Air Commando Wing. Thirty C-47 and C-119 pilots went to the United States in January to convert; the first navigators, fire-control officers and electronic-warfare officers, drawn from the Thu Duc and Dalat classes of 1962–65 and from the VNAF's transport navigators, went in February for about a year. The radar and fire-control technicians were the hardest to find, as the dossier had warned: the technical courses were in English, and the VNAF had perhaps eighty men who could take them in 1967¹².

Mixed crews flew from March, an American instructor pilot and fire-control officer with a Vietnamese crew, and did not work: the Vietnamese crews fought on the province nets in Vietnamese and the instructors deferred or overruled at the wrong moments, and by March 1968 operational sorties were all-Vietnamese. The first all-Vietnamese combat sortie of the 817th Squadron was flown from Bien Hoa on the night of 19–20 August 1967. At 2350 the RF post at Hiep Hoa, on the Vam Co Dong in Duc Hue district, called the district in Vietnamese that it was under attack from the north-east; the Spooky II was over it at 0012, its fire-control officer, Captain Le Minh Tuan, spoke to the post's commander directly, and the 40mm and 105mm broke the assault in the cane north of the post in about twenty minutes, under a cloud base the radar saw through¹². The post lost one man. It was the first time in the war that a Vietnamese post had been defended at night from the air by Vietnamese, and Khiem had the post commander's call played on the wing's loudspeakers at Bien Hoa the next morning.

By December 1967 the 817th had eleven crews and flew about 120 sorties a month over III and IV Corps; the 819th was forming at Nha Trang for the coast, and the 821st had not begun. The cost was in the rest of the VNAF: the A-1 squadrons at Bien Hoa lost about a fifth of their avionics technicians to the gunship wing in 1967, and their aircraft were about two to three points less often operational for it¹².

### New: The night of the relief at My Phuoc Tay
*9–10 Mar 1967 · The PF post at Ap My Loi and the canal road to Cai Lay district town, My Phuoc Tay village, Cai Lay District, Dinh Tuong Province · EV008-4*

*Initiative: enemy*

This is the night the radio's second-order effect became visible, and the night that shows it best. By 1967 every Popular Forces post in the held belt of Dinh Tuong had a set on the district net, a PRC-25 from the Go Vap plant since the previous autumn, and a fresh battery every Thursday from the exchange at the district⁶. The Front had stopped assaulting those posts in 1965, as it had stopped assaulting the rearmed ones. In the first months of 1967 the Dinh Tuong provincial unit decided to use the radio against the men it called.

At 2235 on 9 March a mortar section of the 514th Local Force Battalion put twelve 60mm rounds into the post at Ap My Loi, a mud-walled fort on the canal six kilometres north of Cai Lay, from about 300 metres across the paddy. Sergeant Le Van Muoi, who commanded its PF platoon, called the district at 2237, reported the mortar and an assault forming on the dike to the west, and asked for the reaction force. The assault did not come. Two companies of the 514th were not on the dike at all; they were lying in the sugar cane on both sides of the canal road, three kilometres south of the post, where the road crossed a concrete culvert that the district's trucks had to slow to cross⁶.

The district chief, Major Nguyen Thanh Liem, did what the rule of 1964 told him, that a post that called would have its reaction within the hour, and sent the 247th Regional Force Company north in four trucks at 2250. At 2304 a command-detonated mine under the culvert lifted the lead truck off the road. The firing circuit, the district's engineers found in the morning, was two kilometres of WD-1 field wire from the Republic's own mill and a pack of Go Vap dry cells of the kind the post had been issued the week before. The two companies fired into the other three trucks from both sides for about eight minutes, took the weapons from the first, and were gone into the cane before the 7th Division's battery at Cai Lay had been given a target. The 247th lost 31 dead and 18 wounded and about 40 weapons, most of them M4A1 carbines and two M249s. The post itself lost one man, wounded by the mortar. The district reported 46 of the enemy killed; eight bodies were found at the culvert in the morning, and I believe the 514th lost between ten and fifteen killed⁶.

In this war there was a gunship over Dinh Tuong that night, and the Front had planned for it. At 2220, fifteen minutes before the mortar opened on Ap My Loi, a company of the 261st Main Force Battalion attacked the post at Long Dinh in Chau Thanh district, 25 kilometres east, with mortars and a ground probe, and the Ghostrider of the 4th Squadron on station over the province went there, as the post's call and the district's relay told it to. It was firing on the 261st's company in the rice east of Long Dinh when the mine went off under the culvert at Cai Lay, and by the time it reached the canal road at 2318 the two companies of the 514th were in the cane, moving north-west by squads, and the crew found and fired on only one of them as it crossed the open paddy toward the Plain of Reeds¹². The 514th's dead at the culvert and in the paddy I now put at about 20–30. The 261st's attack at Long Dinh was a diversion, the first the Front had made to draw the gunship off; it was not the last.

Liem wrote new rules the following week, and they are the reason the night belongs in the history. A post's first call would be for fire, not men: every post in the district had its concentrations plotted for the 105mm battery at Cai Lay and the 7th Division's guns at Cai Be, and the call was answered by the guns within four minutes. A relief would move by water or at first light, never by road at night on the one road the Front could predict. And a post that could hold behind its wire would be expected to. The rules spread through IV Corps in the spring, carried by the province advisers and by the 7th Division's artillery officers. In the months that followed, attacks on posts within range of the guns in Dinh Tuong fell by about a third, and the Front's district companies turned to the posts beyond the guns' 11 kilometres and to the posts whose batteries were run down at the end of the exchange week⁶.

The rules had a cost that the returns did not show and Liem's adviser did. A platoon that could call down the guns had less reason to leave its wire after dark, and in 1967 the night patrols of the PF platoons in Cai Lay fell by about a third; the post held itself, and the hamlet outside it was walked at night, more often than before, by the Front's tax collectors⁶. Ap My Loi held every attack made on it for the rest of the war. Whether the hamlet that bore its name was the government's after dark is a question the post's radio log cannot answer.

Sergeant Muoi had passed the leader's course at Nha Trang in 1961 and the platoon leader's course at the Dinh Tuong centre in 1964, and he kept a listening post of two men on the canal bank 300 metres south of the post every night. At 2241 they reported men moving south in the cane on the far side of the canal, toward the road, and Muoi added it to his report: the mortar, an assault forming to the west, and movement south toward the culvert. The district operations room logged it as the third of three lines. Liem read the first two and sent the trucks, because the rule said the reaction within the hour and the post had called; the sergeant had seen the ambush and the decision was not his⁸. The ambush went as told. The third of Liem's new rules came from Muoi's line in the log: a post's report of movement on the relief route stops the relief until the route is fired on or cleared at first light, and the district's posts were taught, through their platoon leaders, to report the road as well as the wire.

Liem's fourth rule came from the night's other lesson. No relief would move by road at night unless a gunship flew the road ahead of it, and the province's two gunship sorties a night were assigned in pairs from April, one over the posts and one held for the road. On the night of 14 June 1967 the 247th RF Company moved north to Ap My Loi again, under a post's call, with a Ghostrider over the canal road two kilometres ahead of the trucks; its turret found about fifty men lying in the cane at the culvert, the trucks stopped, and the 105mm and 30mm fired on the cane for twenty minutes. The 514th left 26 dead and two 57mm recoilless rifles at the culvert, and the 247th reached the post at 0130 without a man hit¹². It did not lay an ambush on that road again on a clear night.

## Phase IV — Vietnamization and drawdown (Jan 1969 – Dec 1971)

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1971 the United States has about 158,000 military personnel in Vietnam, its ground combat role is nearly over, and the last US combat divisions are leaving²¹. The RVNAF numbers more than a million men under arms, well equipped and, in the territorial forces, more present in the hamlets than ever before²⁹. In the countryside the VC remain weaker than at any time since 1960 and weaker in the Delta than on the historical course; the land programme of 1964 has finished its work, with about 1,150,000 hectares titled, and the Land to the Tiller law of 1970 was never needed. The Commission survives below the rank of minister and general and no longer above it¹. These gains are real, and they are measured mostly by indicators the government itself produces.

On the frontiers the balance is the reverse. The PAVN has rebuilt its main forces, extended the Trail in Laos and Cambodia, lost Sihanoukville and replaced it, and watched the ARVN's best divisions fail in Laos without American advisers. The secret channel in Paris is deadlocked on Thieu's removal and on the PAVN's presence in the South. In Hanoi, after Lam Son 719, the Politburo has decided to stake the next year on a conventional invasion across the DMZ, from Laos into the Central Highlands and from Cambodia towards Saigon, timed to an American election year and to the near completion of the American withdrawal³⁰. The question of Phase V is the one Vietnamization was built to answer: whether the South can stop a PAVN conventional offensive with American air power but without American ground troops.

The Board still ranks the candidates and the Prime Minister now chooses the loyal among the competent². The posts, the census and the district Special Branch sections stand, and the historical police has caught up with them in size; what the Republic keeps from 1964 is the chiefs' experience and four extra years of files.

The radar's ledger has made the interdiction debate honest and changed nothing it was about: the Trail is larger at the end of 1971 than ever, the Liberation Route through northeastern Cambodia is mapped and open, and the aircraft that count both will leave with the Americans¹⁶.

The ARVN's I Corps ends the phase believing, on the evidence of Lolo and Sophia, that a besieged base under American bombers holds. It is true, and it is the belief that will cost it most when the bombers go³¹.

Phung Hoang ends 1971 with an audited count of about 63,000 neutralized since 1965 and a national file of about 230,000 names in one building in Saigon, serving the President as well as the war. About 3,500 selected advisers remain, with the territorials and the province teams more than with the divisions; the American battalions have gone home whole and their discipline has decayed on its historical course⁴.

The board ends 1971 as the machinery of the army below colonel and nothing above it: battalions and regiments are commanded by officers it chose, for terms it sets, and the divisions and corps by the President's choices⁵. The colonels who asked for the list back are in the schools and the staffs. The battalions that went into Laos came out of it better than the operation did.

The RVNAF enters 1972 with a closed rebuild loop and a domestic share that covers about two-fifths of its small-arms cartridges, a third of its 105mm rounds and most of its batteries, under a Directorate the palace now runs⁶. The districts of the Delta call Vietnamese guns on Vietnamese sets. Nobody can see the base's weight in a year of free American supply, and it has not yet been tested by a year without it.

The NCO academy at Nha Trang ends 1971 Vietnamese, as it began, with its American advisers gone and its course whole; the gate on promotion has been broken once by decree and half restored by the training command, and about half the sergeants the decree made have taken their course since⁸. The American NCO corps leaves Vietnam schooled and spent, its best sergeants among the dead of the fraggings as well as the fighting.

The 81st Gunship Wing ends 1971 holding the night over about two-thirds of the posts the Ghostriders held, through cloud on the coast where they never could, and in Vietnamese; the posts beyond its reach are attacked more often as the Americans leave¹².
